::: {.at-a-glance}
**Status:** in active use · **Focus:** sound recording, soundscapes, finding species by their calls

**What you get:** bird species found in continuous recordings; soundscape measures that summarise habitat; calls of bats, amphibians and insects.
:::

## What is acoustic monitoring?

Acoustic monitoring uses small, autonomous sound recorders to capture the soundscape: birds, bats, amphibians, insects, mammals and environmental sounds. Unlike imaging systems such as [AMI](ami.qmd), it focuses on **species that are easier to hear than see**, and it can sample continuously over long periods with very little fieldwork.

## Recorders we use

- **AudioMoth**: an ultra-low-cost, open-source autonomous recorder.
- **Song Meter recorders (Wildlife Acoustics)**: high-quality field units for bird and bat surveys.
- **Bat detectors**: for ultrasonic bat monitoring ([more](ultrasonic.qmd)).
- **Custom-built recorders**: specialised units for research projects and long-term observatories.

## Why it matters

- Many species, especially **birds, bats and amphibians**, are best found by sound.
- Recorders can run **continuously**, at all hours.
- They give **non-intrusive**, standardised sampling over long periods.
- They are **portable and inexpensive**, so they can be used widely.
- Recordings are a **permanent archive** that can be re-analysed as models improve.

Acoustic monitoring helps reveal which birds live in a place, how active bats are, when amphibians breed, and how habitat quality changes over time.

## How it works

**Recording:** recorders are set to record continuously or on a schedule, for example the dawn chorus or the night, and run for weeks or months with little maintenance.

**Processing:** AI models, such as BirdNET and Perch for birds and BatDetect2 for bats, find and name the calls. Acoustic indices summarise the whole soundscape. Experts then check a sample, so the species lists can be trusted.

**Results:** species found at each site, how often they call, biodiversity indicators, and evidence for restoration and long-term change. Recordings can also become [videos and soundscapes](https://github.com/NERC-CEH/ceh-biomonitoring#5-visualisation) to share.

Acoustic monitoring sits alongside our imaging systems, so together they give a fuller picture: what is seen, what is heard, and the environmental context.

## Try it

Our [open-source toolkit](https://github.com/NERC-CEH/ceh-biomonitoring) runs the bird and bat models on your own recordings. Partners working with us can [send us their recordings](../how-to/upload.qmd).
